name: EY
summary: EY's interviews lean on behavioural questions, which EY says on its careers site it relies on heavily, alongside technical questions for the service line you've applied to, such as assurance, tax, consulting or strategy and transactions. For campus roles, including at EY Global Delivery Services (GDS), candidates commonly report an aptitude or written test followed by one or more interviews; the steps vary by country, service line and role.
rounds: Online application, with an aptitude or written assessment for many roles
Technical interview for the service line: accounting, tax, technology or analytics
Behavioural interview with a manager, often built on 'give an example of' questions
Final discussion with a senior manager, director or partner (for many roles)
HR conversation on fit, preferences and start date (for some roles)
looks_for: People who demonstrate integrity, respect, teaming and inclusiveness
People with energy, enthusiasm and the courage to lead
People who build relationships based on doing the right thing
Mindset as much as skill set: how you approach challenges and learning
Specific examples: the situation, the action you took and the result

questions.text: Give an example of a time you worked in a team that disagreed on the approach. What did you do?
covers: The disagreement and what each side wanted
Your part in getting the team to a decision, in the first person
The result and how the team worked together afterwards

questions.text: Describe a situation when you took the lead without being asked.
covers: What needed doing and why nobody had picked it up
What you did first and how you brought others along
The outcome, with something concrete

questions.text: Tell me about a time you had to produce accurate work against a tight deadline.
covers: The deadline and why accuracy mattered
How you planned, checked your work and asked for help where needed
What you delivered, and anything you'd do differently

questions.text: Describe a time you pushed back because something wasn't right.
covers: What was wrong and how you were sure
How you raised it respectfully and with evidence
What changed, and how the relationship held up

questions.text: What is the purpose of an external audit, and what does an auditor's opinion tell an investor?
covers: An independent check that financial statements are free of material misstatement
What a clean opinion means, and what a qualified or adverse one signals
That an audit gives reasonable, not absolute, assurance

questions.text: How would you check whether a company's reported revenue is genuine? Name a few tests you'd do.
covers: Matching sales to orders, delivery records and cash received
Cut-off testing around the year end, and confirmations from customers
Looking for unusual patterns such as big sales just before year end or many credit notes after

questions.text: Walk me through how depreciation affects the three financial statements.
covers: It's an expense that lowers profit, and so tax
It reduces the asset's value on the balance sheet
It's added back in the cash flow statement because no cash leaves

questions.text: Explain the difference between direct and indirect taxes, with an example of each from a country you know.
covers: Direct taxes are paid by the person or company taxed, such as income tax
Indirect taxes are collected through prices, such as GST or VAT
Why a business cares about both: cost, compliance and cash flow

questions.text: A client's month-end financial close takes too long. How would you find out what's slowing it down?
covers: Mapping the steps, owners and hand-offs in the close
Finding delays with data: late inputs, manual reconciliations, rework
Quick fixes and longer-term automation, with how you'd measure the gain

questions.text: How would you explain the benefits and risks of moving to the cloud to a client's finance head?
covers: Benefits in their terms: cost, flexibility, faster reporting
Risks: data security, migration effort, ongoing costs, depending on one provider
A sensible first step, such as a small pilot with clear success measures

questions.text: Tell me about a project where you used data to find something others had missed.
covers: The question and the data you worked with
The tools and methods you used (Excel, SQL, Python or others)
What you found and what changed because of it

questions.text: Why EY, and why this service line?
covers: What the service line does and who its clients are
Why the work fits your studies, skills or experience
Something specific about EY you learnt from its people or work

questions.text: EY's purpose is 'Building a better working world'. What could that mean in the role you've applied for?
covers: A plain reading of the purpose, linked to the role
An example: trustworthy numbers, a fairer tax process, or a client system that works better
Why that kind of impact matters to you

questions.text: What questions do you have for us?
covers: Specific questions about the team's clients, the first year or training
A question that shows you've thought about the role
Nothing you could have found on the careers site in a minute

tips: EY's careers pages describe behavioural interviewing: prepare stories on teamwork, deadlines, conflict, a mistake and leadership, and end each on the result.
Revise your service line's basics: audit and accounting for assurance, tax principles for tax, a tool or process for technology consulting.
Match one example to each skill listed in the role description before the interview.
EY describes interviews as two-way; prepare two specific questions about the team's clients or the work you'd do in your first year.
For GDS and other campus roles, be ready to talk in detail about your projects, internships and the tools you list, such as Excel, SQL or a programming language.
